newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-RUSSIA HONOURS LATE SOCCER HERO.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RUSSIA HONOURS LATE SOCCER HERO.

text.p: Four decades late, Russian soccer has paid tribute this week to perhaps the greatest and certainly the most tragic player it ever produced.

The Russian Soccer Federation and the Torpedo Moscow club are running an international veterans' tournament to mark the 60th birthday of Eduard Streltsov, "The Russian Pele" who spent his finest playing years imprisoned in a Siberian Gulag.
When Streltsov died of cancer seven years ago he was mourned by a nation of adoring fans but shunned by Soviet officialdom for a crime his footballing comrades say he did not commit.
The blond and dashing striker made his debut in the national team at just 17 -- the same age as Pele -- scoring a first-half hat-trick in a 6-0 thrashing of Sweden in Stockholm in 1955.

But three years later, on the eve of his opportunity to face the Brazilian genius in the 1958 World Cup finals, the man fans nicknamed "Strelets" (Sharpshooter) found himself charged with rape and sentenced to six years' hard labour.

Just days before the highly-fancied Soviet squad left for Sweden, Streltsov was arrested with team mates Boris Tatushin and Mikhail Ogonkov in connection with the rape of a young woman, said to be the daughter of a high-ranking KGB officer.
Charges against the other two players were dropped but the official Soviet media said Streltsov had broken a team curfew with one of his many female admirers and raped her.

"He was a victim of the time," Valentin Ivanov, Streltsov's long-time partner at Torpedo and the national side, recalled this week. "He was innocent but the Soviet party leaders wanted to make Eduard a scapegoat."

One Russian soccer writer, who was present at Streltsov's trial but even after nearly 40 years would speak only on condition of anonymity, said the young striker was set up by powerful Soviet culture minister, Yekaterina Furtseva.

"Furtseva's daughter was in love with Streltsov and the minister summoned Eduard to the Kremlin asking him to marry the daughter," the writer said, recounting a tale widely accepted in Russian footballing circles.

"Tall, good-looking, with curly blond hair, he was adored by thousands of fans, particularly women, and Streltsov declined the proposition. From then on Furtseva had her mind set on revenge and she used the old methods to get Streltsov.
"Streltsov's problem also was that he just couldn't say no to some of his so-called friends -- too much partying, drinking, lots of women -- he wasted his talent. Too much too soon," said the writer.
Ivanov said the political elite, still living in the shadow of dictator Josef Stalin, who died in 1953, were quick to punish any expression of individual success.
"The prosecution didn't have much of a case," Ivanov said.

But Streltsov still spent the next six years chopping timber in the wilds of Siberia after his comrades went out 2-0 in the World Cup quarter-finals to their Swedish hosts, who went on to lose to Pele and the Brazilians in the final.
"You can understand how much our team missed Eduard in 1958," said Ivanov, who played against Sweden. "With him in the line-up we could easily have made the final against Brazil."
Instead, Streltsov was reduced to being the star attraction of whatever Gulag side the Siberian prison bosses fielded.
Remarkably, however, he managed to return from the camps with much of his soccer skill intact.

"When he came back to big league soccer in 1965 he was still the best player we had," soccer historian Aksel Vartanyan said. That season he led Torpedo to their second Soviet title and was then voted Player of the Year for the next two seasons.
"He will always be remembered as a real fans' favourite," Ivanov said of Streltsov, who retired at the end of the 1970 season. "At last our soccer officials are honouring him too."
